title: What is anxiety?
citation: Penninx, B. W., Pine, D. S., Holmes, E. A., & Reif, A. (2021). Anxiety disorders. Lancet (London, England), 397(10277), 914-927.
content:
What is anxiety?

Anxiety is the mind and body's natural response to detecting possible danger or uncertainty. In small amounts it is helpful, keeping us alert and prepared when something matters. Anxiety becomes a problem when this threat response is activated too often, too strongly, or in situations that are not actually dangerous. It is influenced by a combination of biology, life experiences, personality, and current stress, so there is rarely one single cause.

Isn't anxiety just overthinking?

Many people describe anxiety as "just overthinking", but overthinking is only one part of the experience. Anxiety involves changes throughout the body as well as the mind. The brain becomes more focused on spotting possible threats, while the nervous system prepares for action by increasing alertness and releasing stress hormones. Because anxiety has both physical and psychological components, it is not something that can simply be switched off through willpower.

Why do I feel anxious for no reason?

It is common to feel anxious without being able to identify one clear cause. The brain's threat detection system can become more sensitive after ongoing stress, lack of sleep, difficult life experiences, or a combination of biological and psychological factors. Sometimes the body reacts before the conscious mind has identified what triggered it. Not being able to explain why you feel anxious does not mean the experience is any less real.
